Mary Wollstonecraft. The English writer and philosopher who lived from 1759 to 1797 and whose A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, published in 1792, became foundational to feminist thought.

In that revolutionary treatise, Wollstonecraft rejected the notion that women were naturally suited to domestic submission. She argued that women's subordination was imposed by law and custom, not inscribed in nature. Women were not naturally inferior to men, she insisted. Rather, they were denied education and independence, denied the opportunity to develop as rational beings.

Wollstonecraft made a case for women's educational and political equality grounded in Enlightenment philosophy. She insisted that women needed education not to ornament themselves for men, but to become independent rational beings and citizens. This education, she argued, was necessary for a rational society.

She lived an unconventional life that embodied her principles. She worked as a governess, lady's companion, and teacher before becoming a writer, defying eighteenth-century expectations of female propriety. She traveled to revolutionary France during the Terror. She had a daughter out of wedlock with an American diplomat named Gilbert Imlay, challenging sexual and social norms directly through her own life. She later married philosopher William Godwin, but died at thirty-eight from complications of childbirth. Her daughter, Mary Shelley, inherited her legacy of intellectual defiance and wrote Frankenstein.
